title: Computational strategy for the Gröbner--Shirshov normal form
html:
Remark. Computational strategy for the Gröbner--Shirshov normal form

The Gröbner--Shirshov normal form computation separates into three complexity regimes.

The three regimes

Regime 1: Transfer matrix (O(A^2)). The optimal normal form \{\mathbf{1}, \sigma_0, \ldots, \sigma_{A-2}\} possesses coefficients equal to the Markov-traced volumes \hat{V}_i(q). Each \hat{V}_i is a product of A - i - 1 transfer matrices T(c_j, d_j). This requires \binom{A}{2} multiplications. This yields the Q-value, the Skein polynomial, and the optimal normal form coefficients without Iwahori--Hecke algebra expansion.

Regime 2: Symbolic Gröbner--Shirshov with stripping (O(A^3)). The full normal form dictates the Pauli factor F_{\mathrm{Pauli}}, the color content, and the per-length weight distribution. We apply inductive quotient stripping with ideals I_{8} and I_{9} after each strand. This bounds the intermediate term count to O(A^2) per strand, yielding O(A^3) overall. All coefficients remain exact Laurent polynomials in \mathbb{Z}[t, t^{-1}].

Regime 3: Full expansion (O(A!)). Without stripping, the raw normal form generates up to A! terms. This limits tractability to A \leq 9. The full expansion exposes the raw histogram and palindromic structure. It contributes to no physical observable.

Inductive quotient chaining

We apply the chain collapse ideal I_{9} at each strand boundary. We accumulate the Pauli data of stripped terms as symbolic polynomials. The surviving optimal basis contains roughly A terms. The subsequent strand computation initiates from these A terms, bypassing the A! explosion.

The accumulation is exact. Each stripped term contributes its coefficient c_w(t) to the running totals \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{alt}}(t) and \mathrm{net}(t). We weight this by (-t^{-2})^{\ell(w)} for the alternating trace. The final witness sums the accumulated stripped and surviving contributions.

We accumulate only stripped terms. If we accumulated all terms before stripping, surviving terms would double-count when contributing to subsequent strands.

The bottleneck: strand 8

For nuclei with A > 8, the computation exhibits a characteristic bottleneck:

  1. Strands 1–7: The normal form builds to \sim 14{,}000 terms at A = 8, or \sim 230{,}000 terms at A = 9. This takes under 10 seconds.
  2. Strand 8 boundary: The I_{9} strip collapses \sim 230{,}000 terms to roughly 9 terms. We accumulate the Pauli data for the stripped terms.
  3. Strands 9+: Each strand expands from \sim 10 terms to 5{,}000–240{,}000 terms. It then strips back to 10–600 terms at the boundary.

The bottleneck is the final crossing of a large strand. This typically involves neutron–neutron crossings characterized by c = 1, d = -(q - q^{-1}). Peak memory occurs immediately before stripping.

Optimisation strategies

Monomial ordering (LenLex). We use length-lexicographic ordering. The engine reduces shorter words first, then applies lexicographic ordering within the same degree. This aligns with the Iwahori--Hecke algebra. The Hecke relation \sigma_i^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + 1 acts as the sole degree-changing rule.

Junction-only reduction. When appending \sigma_k to a reduced word w, we check only the junction. The prefix w remains reduced. This lowers the amortized per-word reduction cost from O(\ell) to O(1).

Separated reduction pools. We partition terms into stable fully-reduced and pending pools. We never rescan stable terms. When a pending term collides with a stable term, the merged result returns to the pending pool.

Batch quotient stripping (O(A \cdot L_{\max})). The I_{9} strip processes all terms at each length level simultaneously. It descends from longest to shortest words. We collect and remove all terms containing a specific length \ell - 1 prefix. This operates in O(n \cdot L_{\max}) rather than O(n^2).

Mid-crossing stripping. For large strands, the quotient strip fires within a crossing multiplication once the term count exceeds 30,000. This halts the exponential blowup from cascaded adjacent generators.

Pattern discovery. At each strand boundary, the engine identifies frequent suffix patterns. These candidate sub-words suggest structural ideals beyond I_{8} and I_{9}. Persisting patterns indicate universal structural operations eligible for inclusion in the quotient ideal.

Scalability

A Strategy Time Memory Coefficients
\leq 9 Full expansion \leq 30s \leq 562MB \leq 10^{12}
10–12 Inductive stripping 10–45s \leq 2.5GB \leq 10^{17}
13–16 Inductive + mid-crossing est. 1–5min \leq 3GB \leq 10^{22}
17–20 Needs big integer est. 5–30min \leq 5GB > 10^{38} (i128 overflow)
\leq 40 Transfer matrix only < 1s < 1MB O(A^2)

The transfer matrix operates in O(A^2) and yields Q-values for any A. The symbolic engine supplies F_{\mathrm{Pauli}} and color content up to A \leq 16 in minutes. It extends to A \leq 20 with big integers. Beyond A = 20, exact-in-q calculations overflow. We employ a per-length accumulation float engine instead.
